utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, good morning, everyone. We resume the Prosecution case this morning. So who is to undertake that task?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: The next Prosecution witness is Mr. Mahmut Halimi. Mr. Halimi is one of our Mitrovica witnesses, and he's a live witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Kravetz. Let's have Mr. Halimi brought into court, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: While the witness is being brought in, I would like to indicate that the paragraphs to which this witness's evidence relates are paragraphs 72(f), 73, and 77 of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Halimi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to tell the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Mr. Halimi, as you know, the system here involves the counsel who represent the Prosecution and the various accused asking questions of you. The Court may occasionally ask questions, but generally speaking it will be the representatives of the parties who question you. And the first person to do that will be for the Prosecutor, Ms. Kravetz. Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Could you please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: My name is Mahmut Halimi.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Where and when were you born, Mr. Halimi?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: I was born on the 7th of April, 1954, in the village of Zhabar, municipality of Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what is your profession, Mr. Halimi?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: I have graduated in law and now I'm a lawyer in Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Where were you living in March 1999?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: In March 1999, I was living in Street Ceta e Minatoreve number 9 in Mitrovica, which after the war, unfortunately, is called the northern part of Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Which neighbourhood exactly of Mitrovica is this located -- this street located in?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: This is close to the Kodro e Minatoreve, the miner's hill, in the northern part of Mitrovica, in Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You stated that in March you were living in Mitrovica. Did you at some point that month have to leave your home in the town of Mitrovica? You have to speak your answer into the microphone, Mr. Halimi.

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes. I left my home on the 25th of March of 1999 at about 6.30, a quarter to 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could you briefly tell the Court why you left your home on the 25th of March.

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes. Because a lady called me at about 6.00 in the morning. She spoke in Serbian. This was on the 25th of March. And she advised me to leave my home as soon as possible. And she said, I quote, "Leave as soon as possible. You don't know what -- what's waiting for you. You don't know what has happened. Leave your home." So then I took my wife, my four children, my mother at that time was 75 years old, and we all left in a very short time, and we went in the direction of Zhabar, my village of birth. It's about 3 kilometres from Mitrovica in the western part.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Where did you stay when you went to the village of Zhabar?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: My oldest brother lives there, my eldest brother; I went to his house together with my family and we joined his family. That's where I stayed, in his house.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You mentioned that you had received a phone call from this woman who told you that you didn't know what was happening and that you should leave the house. When you got to Zhabar, did you find out anything that was happening in Mitrovica, why this woman had called you?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: First of all I'd like to link this with a moment when I crossed the Ibar River and went to the new station of the town of Mitrovica. The same woman called me and she said: Have you left already, because they have approached your home? I think she was talking about the military and paramilitary forces. I told her that I had gone across the river. And after I went to Zhabar, I learned that the night of the 24th and 25th of March Agim Hajrizi had been killed at his own home.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: It's no problem --

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I know this is difficult for you. Mr. Halimi, you were telling us that you --

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: This was my collaborator. He was a very hard-working person, and he contributed a lot to the future of Kosova. He was a very close friend of mine. He was killed together with his mother and his youngest son, who at the time was 12 or 13 years old. He was not 13. And also Mr. Latif Berisha, a professor at the University of Pristina, and he was also chairman of the LDK in Mitrovica. That's how I learned what had happened in Zhabar. I learned what had happened between the 24th and the 25th of March, that night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Halimi, when you describe Agim Hajrizi as your collaborator, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, he was head of the trade unions of the Trepca union, while I was a lawyer and I represented the interests of that trade union.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You were in private practice as a lawyer in March 1999?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Halimi, you said that you went to the village of Zhabar. For how many days did you remain there?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: I stayed there for two days. The third day I had to leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Why did you have to leave?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: I had to leave because, according to the information I got from citizens in Tavnik -- from Tavnik of Mitrovica, the security forces had been looking for me. Two members of the liberation army who introduced themselves to me as such, they had civilian clothes on and they were not armed I think because I did not see any guns on them. And they told me that for your own safety and for the safety of the villagers who are living here now, you have to leave for a day or so. You have to leave the village. So at about 8.00 in the evening, we left -- I mean these two people, these two members of the liberation army, the names of whom I don't know. I remember their faces, and also my brother --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The sons of my -- two sons of my brother, so there were six of us altogether. We went to the mountains of Zhabar, which was about 4 kilometres from the place where I was. So I went to the mountain.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Halimi, you said that two members of the KLA contacted you. Was the KLA present in the village of Zhabar?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: I could say that they were there time after time to avoid the risks that were -- that were presented to the villagers by the Serbian forces. There were no armed forces, but there was this clinic of the KLA led by Dr. Bajram Rexhepi, who was a surgeon, and he treated there both civilians and soldiers who had gotten wounded in various places where there was fighting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You just told us that you went to the mountains with other members of your family and these two KLA soldiers. Did you at some point return to Zhabar?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Maybe it's a misinterpretation. I did not go with my family to the mountains. My wife and children stayed in Zhabar, but it was my brother's sons that came with me to the mountains and I stayed there for six days with them. And I then went back to my family later.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And once you returned to Zhabar, for how many more days did you remain there with your family?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: I stayed there until the 14th of April, 1999. That day at about 10.00 -- because I have to explain here. My brother's house is very close to the Ibar River, and it looks over Suhadoll and the new stadium on the other side of the river. You have a very good view there, and we were watching and observing. There were other people as well watching and observing because they feared for their lives. From Suhadoll, the Serbian forces came towards the stadium, the new stadium. I saw two APCs which at that time started to shoot with their machine-guns. I had been a soldier myself some time ago, but I had never seen such guns. Their names were Pragas. This was a very sad noise, and they were shooting in the direction of the village, upper part of the village. There were four to six shots fired from the APCs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You said you saw Serb forces firing at the village of Zhabar. Can you describe anything about the forces you saw there in terms of the uniform they were wearing? Were you able to see this from where you were?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: From the distance I was staying, I can't say I could see their uniforms because although there is no obstacle to the view, it's about 1 kilometre away. But as I said, I saw the APCs and somebody was driving them, the Serbian forces were. I did not see the uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: How did you and your family react once the village of -- once the Serb forces started firing on the village of Zhabar?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: What else could I do? I wanted to leave because my youngest children, my son was 5, my daughter was 7, my mother was 75 years old. So I had to leave lower Zhabar and went in the direction of upper Zhabar. I was able to go along the Ibar River, and I went to the house that was closest to the forest, to the mountain in that village, upper Zhabar. My brother came, too, with his family, and we stayed there until the 17th of April. I think it was the 16th, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You said you observed this firing on the 14th of April and that you went to upper Zhabar. The following day, were you able to observe anything unusual when you were there in upper Zhabar?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: From the place I was staying, at the upper part of the village, there was about 400 metres above the rest of the village. I could see lower Zhabar. I could see part of Mitrovica and Tavnik, and also part of the village Shipol as well as the road Mitrovica-Peje 300 metres from the water supply company, which is above the village of Shipol. That day it was the 15th of April, 1999, at about 10.00 or 10.30. I could see -- but other people who were with me could see as well, that the population was moving en masse in Zhabar, people coming from the direction of Suhadoll, which is in the north-eastern part from Mitrovica, the neighbourhood of Tavnik, which is to the east of Zhabar. So these people were coming towards the west. And from Shipol, also people were coming towards Zhabar. Shipol is also to the north-east of Zhabar. And this was movement en masse of people on foot, and after 11.30 or 12.00 more people were moving and it was a very sad sight. This mass of people moving and at 2.00 p.m. or 2.30 p.m. -- so the village of Zhabar which is about 150 square kilometres, it was full of people. You could not see the earth, the soil, because of the people who were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You stated that you began in the morning seeing a mass of people moving towards Zhabar. Do you -- were you able to observe why these people were coming in the direction of Zhabar?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Because in the places that I mentioned, Shipol, Tavnik, part of Mitrovica, and Suhadoll, the Serbian forces had entered those areas, I mean the military forces, the police forces, and they had been expelling people, terrorising people. There were also people who were killed, because on the 14th and 15th of April in Rrhga e Kovaceve, over 26 Albanians were killed, all young people, with the exception of one who was 52 years old. And as a result of this distress and this situation, the people wanted to go to a safer place.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You said that the Serb forces were expelling or -- these people, forcing these people to leave. Was this something you were able to observe yourself from upper Zhabar or how did you find this out, that this was happening?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Well, I experienced myself the golgotha. I knew and everybody knew that people came all the time. People from lower Zhabar were coming to upper Zhabar where I was and were telling us that the army, the police, and the paramilitaries had been expelling them from their homes, and that's why they had to come to Zhabar.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When you say -- when you said that you saw a mass of people coming, how many people do you think or do you estimate that had been forced out of Mitrovica that day?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Later, as I was following the situation, which if you allow me I will explain very briefly and I will tell you how I came up with the approximate number of the inhabitants that had left. Your Honours and Mrs. Prosecutor, it was about 1600 hours. This mass of people became a convoy and --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you there. You said this mass of people became a convoy. Is this something that happened -- these people came to Zhabar and this is something that happened when they came to Zhabar that they -- that you said they became a convoy? What do you mean exactly?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes. They came to Zhabar and when they were leaving Zhabar the convoy was formed in the main road.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Were you able to observe in which direction this convoy headed?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes. It went in the direction of the Peje road in the direction of Shipol, the Mitrovica-Peje main road, and there are two roads there that lead from the crossroads at lower Zhabar. One goes towards the school in Shipol, the other one goes to the school in Shipol as well, but it's a longer way. And the two roads join together at the school. So the people who were on foot were going in this -- on this straight road towards the primary school in Shipol, while the cars were going along the other road, which was the longer one. And then the two joined together at the school. And there were so many people on foot that the road was not enough for them to walk on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When this was happening, that these people were moving towards this school in Shipol, did you see any Serb forces present in Zhabar?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes. I saw Serb forces that were there. There were paramilitary forces who were stationed at Valoni Hotel in lower Zhabar. The hotel is about 50 metres from the main road. During that time, especially between 1430 and 1600 hours, shots were heard from different kinds of weapons. Later on I learned that three inhabitants of Zhabar village had been killed on that day. Several vehicles were burned, and I saw this myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You said that you saw paramilitary forces there. What exactly do you mean by paramilitary forces? Can you describe what sort of uniforms these paramilitary forces were wearing?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes. You could distinguish paramilitary forces from military and police ones as per their clothes, uniforms, and equipment that they were carrying. They wore scarves, bandannas on their heads, not caps. The majority of them were -- had their heads shaved and had beards, and they left this impression of fear and terror. Their weapons were very sophisticated ones. They were carrying long-barrel weapons between 1 metre 40 to 1 metre 60. They were sniper rifles with small magazines. So this is how we could tell that these were paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: In addition to these forces that you describe as paramilitary, did you see any other men in uniform in Zhabar when this -- these events were taking place?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Ms. Prosecutor, from very close I had the opportunity to see them on --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the date.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] April between 9.00 and 11.15 in the morning --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the interpreter wasn't able to catch the date that you're describing that you were able to see these forces.

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: It was 15th of April -- excuse me, it was 16th of April, 1999. It was after 11.00, maybe 11.20, when, as I explained in my statement, the Serb forces managed to force the column from lower Zhabar to take the Peje road and continue moving in the direction of Peje along the Peje road. This happened, and I saw this with my own eyes when on the road that I described earlier near the Shipol primary school the last -- even the last vehicle was burned. This was around 11.00. This is when the Serb forces entered there, the police, the paramilitary forces, and military, regular military forces. As Zhabar e Eperm, or upper Zhabar, is divided into the flat part and the hilly part, these forces entered and they started to burn the houses, they started to burn houses in the lower part. We could see the smoke coming out of the houses and we could hear shooting. The villagers left the flat part of the village. There were also other displaced persons who had moved to Zhabar from other areas, not only Zhabar inhabitants there. They joined the column and went to what we call Gaterat. It is a carpentry compound. I saw them going there with my own eyes. Soon after --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Is this a different group of people -- you said the first group of people had been sent in the direction of Shipol. Now you're speaking of a group sent in a direction of a carpentry --

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes, yes, another group because, as I said, the other group continued along the Peje road in the column. Those from Zhabar e Ulet, those that joined the column in the evening and that stayed in a column all night long, they continued in the direction of Peje. Now immediately after the expulsion of the upper Zhabar, the flat part of upper Zhabar began. Four houses, three or four houses were burnt there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: What did you do --

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: So they left and they went to this carpentry compound. That's when I realised that I had no way out because the same thing was going to happen to us; that's why I decided and I proposed to my brother, because we were together, to leave --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: May I interrupt you there. You said that they -- the Serb forces had started burning houses in the lower part of upper Zhabar and that you decided to leave. Where did you go when you decided to leave, in which direction? Just very briefly, Mr. Halimi.

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: As soon as I saw the people leaving from the lower part of the village, I took this decision immediately. My brother with his family and my brother-in-law, whose wife was pregnant at that time, joined me. We set out in three cars. When we were about to join the main road Mitrovica-Zubin Potok that goes to Montenegro, we were stopped by two soldiers, soldiers of the Yugoslav army. They were very young; I will never forget their faces. One of them was shaking because of fear. We were ordered to get out of the cars. As this soldier came close to me, I remember telling him, and I quote: "You don't have to be scared. We're all civilians. We're trying to save our lives." And he, at least to me, seemed to calm down a little bit, and he allowed me to go back to the car and continue because, as I said, my children were very young. My mother was very old and she was ill. However, they didn't allow me to keep the car. I was allowed to get some elementary things from the car. The military forces began to enter the upper part of the village. I will never forget the following. As we were allowed to leave on the right side of the road, these two small lorries were there, and there I noticed five or six paramilitaries. I could tell they were paramilitaries, and I explained why earlier. I had seen them before at the hotel in Zhabar. There was also a military jeep and a machine-gun on the top. Others were taking things from abandoned houses, and they were loading these things on these two lorries parked nearby. These paramilitaries had bandannas, black bandannas; medium to long beards; they had this dark-colour uniform. It could be even black but I'm not quite sure because it was very difficult to notice all these things under those circumstances. They had -- this particular person had a black T-shirt and he was holding two knives in his hand. We passed by --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: May I interrupt you there, Mr. Halimi, just going back a bit. You said all the other people had been sent to a school in Shipol and to a carpentry compound. What happened to those people? Where did they go after they were sent in this direction?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: These are the people that I already described from Zhabar e Ulet or lower Zhabar. Those who were made a column on the 15th of April and who were forced to stay, to spend the night in the open until the following day when they were forced to continue along the Peje main road. You asked me earlier how many there were. On the basis of the length of the column, of the two columns, the one of the persons on foot and the other of vehicles, I would estimate that there were about 25.000 to 30.000 people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did you eventually join this column of people that was heading down the Peje road?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: No. We left the following day. They left on the 16th, while we who were at upper Zhabar, we spent that night in the carpentry compound. And the following day, that is on the 17th of April, 1999, before noon, the police came and they ordered us to make a column in three minutes and to leave. We had no other way out. Within these three minutes the column was formed and we continued along the road that goes to Peje.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: In -- so once you took the road that -- in the direction of Peje, where exactly did you head in this column? Where did the column head to? Just very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: To Albania. Every column that would set out in that direction, the final destination of those columns was Albania.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recall through which municipalities you went while you were heading to Albania?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes. Mitrovica. We passed near Skenderaj, Klina e Eperme, Klina e Poshteme, Rakosh village, Istog municipality, Gjurakoc. In Gjurakoc we were ordered to go to the left of the road. We continued the road towards Klina. We reached the Klina bridge where the crossroads are, where the road to Gjakova is. Then Prizren, Zhur, and Morina, the border crossing between Kosova and Albania.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: How long did it take you to get from Mitrovica to the border with Albania?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Thanks to my brother's son-in-law, who was a mechanic by profession, we were lucky. There were people who had left their vehicles behind due to some defects or for whatever reason. He found this Golf and a Moskvitch make vehicles. I drove the Golf. I had about eight or nine passengers in my car. My brother and his son-in-law were in the Moskvitch and I was towing the Moskvitch. So we drove in the direction of the border, and we arrived there -- we arrived at Zhur village, that is close to the border with Albania at around 7.00, 7.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Can you --

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Please allow me to say this. Along the road we saw members of the column that had left on the 16th from Zhabar village, those who had left on foot.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Halimi, you were telling us you saw --

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: No problem. I understand. You said you saw members of the column who had left on foot as you were heading to the border?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Many of them, many of them, on both sides of the road, continuously. That was a long, long convoy, full of people on both sides of the road.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: What happened when you reached the border, Mr. Halimi? Were you able to cross it with no problems?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: No, because the column was moving very slowly. From 7.00 to 10.00 p.m. we walked only for some 20 or 50 metres. After approximately 10.00 p.m., I might not know the exact time, it could have been even 11.00 p.m., we heard a very powerful explosion. All of us who were in the column, we thought that it was a NATO bomb and we were just anticipating now the moment when the Serb forces will throw themselves on us to retaliate. The column stopped moving. We spent the night there, and the next day, on the 18th, at around 11.00 -- I mean 18th of April, the column began to move in the direction of the Albanian border. So I managed to come to the border crossing myself. There there were these three boxes or chests, rather. ID cards were supposed to be thrown in one of the chests because the police there said: If we find passports, ID cards, licences in any of you, you will be executed on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Is this something the police told you personally or did you hear this from others?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The window of my car was open. We were moving in a very low speed, and they were passing by every car and warning us. So before reaching the border itself at 10 or 15 metres from the border, the police would come to all of us and tell us that we were obliged to leave the documents and the registration plates of the cars at the border. I would say that it was not in a chest where they threw the registration plates; it was rather a heap, it resembled a hill of registration plates. One of the chests was for the ID cards and the other one for driving licences.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So did you proceed to hand over your ID documents and the licence plates of the cars that you were driving?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: I handed over the registration plates. I handed over the ID card, the drivers licence. Luckily, but it wasn't on purpose since my passport was together with the documents of my children with my wife, when my wife took these documents out of her bag to throw them in the chest, my passport by accident remained in her bag. Otherwise, all of us were supposed to throw the documents in these chests.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You said you saw police, Serb police here at the border who instructed you to hand over your documents. As you were travelling to the border in this convoy, did you see any other Serb forces along the way?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes. Not very far from the border, that is to say, on the left side, the mountainous part and the lower part, they were all secured with regular forces. So the army was on these parts, while on the border-line, on the border crossing, there was the regular police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When you said the army was in these parts, can you describe anything about the type of uniforms you saw on these soldiers or this army wearing, if you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Prosecutor. I completed my regular military service with the Yugoslav army, and I've also completed the school for reserve officers. So I know Yugoslav army uniforms very well. The army wore camouflage green uniforms with olive-green-grey pattern. It is this colour that resembles a leaf, a leaf that is getting yellow. I don't know how to describe it better.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Halimi, did you return to Mitrovica after the war?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And in what condition did you find your home once you returned there?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: I returned on the 11th of July, 1999. A few days after my arrival, I could go and see my house. It was completely burned, and this is the state you will find it in even today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Was it the only house in your neighbourhood burned, or were other houses in -- or had other houses in the neighbourhood also been burnt down?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: In that neighbourhood, in Ceta e Minatoreve Street, my house was the only one that had been burnt, no other house had been burnt. In the upper part, in the direction of the miner's hill, Kodro e Minatoreve, there were another five or six houses that had been burnt. These are still neighbours, but they are in the upper part of the neighbourhood. So in that close neighbourhood where my house was, the only house burnt was my house.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Were you able to find out who had burnt down your house?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Honestly, I did not want to know, but I know this, that the Milosevic regime and the people who followed him and I think the accused who are here have great responsibility. They should be held accountable because these were things that were caused because of their actions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Was there a mosque in Mitrovica prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Was this mosque undamaged before you left Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: There were four mosques in Mitrovica, and now there are only three. All four of them were destroyed. The fourth one was on the right part at the -- on the bank, almost on the bank of the Ibar River. And it had been razed to the ground. Nothing had remained of this mosque, and the situation is the same today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Were you able to find out once you had returned to Mitrovica who had razed this mosque to the ground?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: To my disappointment I heard that -- that there were some Serbian firms and -- or companies and also Serb citizens who had contributed to razing it to the ground. I heard this from some people who had remained in Mitrovica the whole time, and it is also thought that there is a mass grave in there, on that site. And the Serbs had done that to conceal what they had done. And the investigators of the Tribunal could not go there on-site because it is on that part of the Ibar River, north of the city, across the bridge. And I think that had been done deliberately.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I want to move to a different subject, and it's my last set of questions for you. After you returned to Mitrovica -- you had told us that you were practicing as a lawyer before the war. After you returned to Mitrovica, did you take up a position as a judge in the local court?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: As you might know, the United Nations established the interim administration there to govern Kosova, and in the framework of this government, the courthouse started functioning on the 1st of September, 1999. We began our work in the building that existed before, in the northern part, and I was also appointed there together with other people. I worked there for 22 months.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: In your capacity as a judge at the local municipal court of Mitrovica, did you -- were you involved in the case regarding the murder of Agim Hajrizi, who you mentioned earlier in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes. I was chairman of the collegium in the case where -- where two people were charged Lazar Gligorovski and Nenad Pavicevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: The outcome was this: Mr. Lazar Gligorovski, who was charged for aiding and abetting a murder because it was a triple murder, he was released because of lack of evidence, while Mr. Nenad Pavicevic, I couldn't even call him mister. His hands are bloody. I remember him from his childhood, and he used to be my client a long time ago. And I think his hands are steeped in blood, and he has to be account -- has to be accountable for what he has done. He was sentenced in absentia with 20 years' imprisonment, and he is living today in Belgrade and he is leading a very good life with things that he has looted from Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Are you aware of whether Nenad Pavicevic took part in any other crimes other than the murder of Mr. Hajrizi during the war in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes. There is a lot of evidence and there are many witnesses. In Milosevic's case, one witness who came here, Halit Barani, he had recordings and other material evidence, including witnesses. And these show that in addition to the murder of Mr. Agim Hajrizi together with his son and mother, he also is responsible for other murders as well. With his collaborator Ratko Antonijevic, Boban --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if counsel's question is meant to elicit testimony from this witness about what other witnesses may or may not have said in other proceedings I think it is fully improper and I ask that it be stricken or limited in this regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I was only asking if he had personal information about whether Nenad Pavicevic had participated in other crimes. I wasn't asking about the testimony of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you accept the objection is valid to the line that's now being -- at least to the material that the witness is now giving it. So let's have the next question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: In -- Mr. Halimi, are you aware of what was the occupation of Nenad Pavicevic, what was his employment?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: He was a policeman in Mitrovica all the time, working at the police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Halimi.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions at this stage for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Halimi, there are -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Halimi, a couple of things you can perhaps clarify for me. You said that when the two families set off that you had three vehicles and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- you then told us about the two Serb soldiers, young soldiers who had stopped you. You indicated that your vehicle had been taken from you. What happened to the other two vehicles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All three were taken away, mine, my brother's, and his son-in-law's vehicle. And they allowed us then to continue on foot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When your brother got the other two vehicles going for you that you actually travelled to Albania in, where did he locate these vehicles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was his son-in-law. It was the 17th when we were ordered to join the convoy, and we started on foot. We were 400 to 500 metres away from the Shipol school, and this happened when we reached the school. People had left their cars behind. They had broken down for different reasons --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's okay. I just want to know where --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were five or six vehicles there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You have answered that question. You -- I just want to be clear that there's not a translation difficulty in one aspect of your evidence. You referred to upper Zhabar and lower Zhabar. And then when you were talking of upper Zhabar, you talked about the flat part or the lower part and the hilly part. Now, is upper Zhabar divided into two separate identifiable areas known as the flat part and the hilly part?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're right. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And you told us of four mosques in Mitrovica. You said that all four were destroyed, but you set one of them apart. It's not been replaced. It remains that way. Were the other three rebuilt?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, after the war they were rebuilt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And lastly, I didn't understand your reference to the location of the fourth one being inaccessible to the Tribunal's investigating staff. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that it's close to the -- the Ibar bridge which divides the northern part from the southern part of the town. From the end of the war, there has been turmoil there, confrontations. There were problems all the time, to this day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On what basis do you say that the investigating staff of the Tribunal have not been able to visit that location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For security reasons, for safety reasons, because the Serbs won't allow them to go there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you speculating about that or do you know that for a fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can say I know this, I'm sure about this, because I worked as a judge for 22 months and I also had contacts with investigators from the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what you are saying is that this is a no-go area in Kosovo which is under the control of Serb people who will not allow Tribunal staff to investigate there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is what I think and many other Albanian citizens have the same opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Hannis, I -- I dare say you can't clarify this at the moment for us, but it's -- that sounds to me like a matter that ought to be clarified and that we should know whether in fact this is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You're right on both counts, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. We will follow the indictment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- in this case, and the Milutinovic Defence does not have any questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I actually don't have any questions, but I would actually like to clarify the questions that you put. So perhaps we can see if there's any square metre of land in Kosovo where you cannot have access to. I know that there are areas where we don't have access to, but I don't know if there are any where you don't have access to. Do we understand each other? How do you mean that the forces cannot cross into --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on a second. My only reason for asking these questions was because of the reference to a mass grave, not to any -- now, I doubt very much if you're going to make any progress in your venture with the witness, and bearing in mind that I've asked the Prosecution to investigate it, do you think that you're really likely to make progress by these questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can because I know my colleague from earlier. We're colleagues. He's a lawyer, I'm a lawyer. He was a judge and I appeared before him in cases. So we can understand each other, and I even have cases that I'm defending there now. Nothing has changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to ask you the following. I agree that it is your opinion that certain investigations cannot be carried out on the Serbian side, like we call it conditionally -- but anyway I will withdraw that. On that side of the bridge, but to actually assert it's like that, it's a little bit stretched, don't you think? What do you think? Is there a metre over there somewhere that these people have not passed through, I'm meaning the members of the international forces? You know that there are conflicts on bridges. There was an Albanian child in a roll-neck, polo neck, that threw something and we know that there are things like that, but you are telling us that the international forces are unable to cross the bridge and find what they are looking for? This is the only thing that I wanted to ask you, but when I'm appearing in your courtrooms, I don't think that you're a bad judge or anything like that. That is not what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm happy to see my colleague here. I have known him for a long time. I said that the reasons are reasons of safety. My wish is that no victims be found there. That would be my greatest satisfaction, if no body is found there. But from the end of the war and on, people have insisted because of various information that they -- pieces of information that they have received, that there might be bodies there. There are many citizens that are still missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to thank the witness, and I wanted to use the opportunity to greet him. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fila. Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Halimi. I'm Norman Sepenuk, and I'm one of the attorneys for General Ojdanic. You mentioned that after you returned to Mitrovica you took a position as a judge in the interim administration to governing Kosovo. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And you held that position for some 22 months, correct?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And one of the trials that you sat on was a trial in the district court in the year 2000 involving, as you said, Lazar Gligorovski and Nenad Pavicevic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And you were the Presiding Judge in that case, were you not, sir?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I said it earlier that I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And the -- and the -- that case was to determine the guilt or innocence concerning the murder of Agim Hajrizi. Is that correct? You have to say -- you can't just shake your head. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Right. And as I understand it, Mr. Hajrizi was a very close friend of yours?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes. I could say close collaborator, close associate, because I explained to you earlier when the Milosevic regime expelled workers in 1990 in Trepca, there were about 3.500 workers and I represented them with a team of lawyers, volunteers. And I considered him an associate because he was the chairman of the trade unions, and we collaborated very closely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I understand. He was a collaborator and a very close friend and you were obviously very moved by his death; is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes, but it did not affect the way I administered justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Oh, so you felt that even though he was a friend and a close collaborator and that as you described it the person who was eventually found guilty of killing him had blood on his hands, a person whose name you didn't even want to pronounce, you didn't want to call him mister, under those circumstances you say you could be fair and objective in judging the guilt or innocence of Mr. Nenad Pavicevic. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes. I was very fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Did the appointing authority know when they appointed you that you were a very close friend of Mr. Hajrizi? Did they ask you about whether or not you knew Mr. Hajrizi? Did you tell them that?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: All the citizens in Mitrovica knew about our relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That wasn't my question. You were appointed -- who appointed you to be the presiding judge of this court?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: It was Bernard Kouchner at the time. He was the one to appoint the first group of judges after the entering of NATO forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And did Bernard Kouchner know that you were a very close friend and collaborator of Mr. Hajrizi?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: I don't think he asked, but we also did not inform him, we did not think it was important because we had made an oath as judges to administer fair justice to all citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Pavicevic was in absentia; he was not at the trial. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: But he had lawyers there representing him as I understand it. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes, there were lawyers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Did the lawyers representing him know that you were a very close friend and collaborator of Mr. Hajrizi?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes, because they were from Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And they raised no objection to your being on that case?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: No. You can see the minutes of the hearings. No, there was no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And as a matter of fact, Mr. -- Mr. Pavicevic was also a former client of yours. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And you saw no problem, no conflict of interest - as we lawyers call it - by sitting as a judge to judge the guilt or innocence of a person who used to be your client? You saw nothing improper or wrong or unethical about that? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: I don't think that there was a problem as you described it, because I knew Mr. Pavicevic the same as I knew Agim. And I considered him earlier as a friend and they were neighbours, next-door neighbours with Agim Hajrizi. And I represented him in a divorce case four or five years before 1999. I don't think there was any conflict of interest there or violation of ethics, because it was something that had to do with him and his wife. They had been divorced and they wanted to divide their property amongst themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So on the one hand you considered him as a friend and on the other hand you considered him as somebody with blood on his hands whose name you did not want to even pronounce. Is that correct? You're shaking your head, does that mean no, yes?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes, but then when he chose the road of crime, especially by the end of 1998 and the whole of 1999, I did not have any contact whatsoever with him and there was no friendship anymore because of his hands full of blood.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Just one or two final questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: When Mr. Kouchner appointed you to become a judge, did he make any investigation of your background as a judge in Mitrovica when you were younger and as a defence lawyer? Did he ever make any investigation to your knowledge about your background?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Of course he must have done. Maybe the OSCE in the beginning, the regional office in Mitrovica --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Was the subject of bribery ever discussed?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: What do you mean? I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: What I mean is that in the Milosevic case you admitted to Judge May in answer to a question that you were involved in bribery countless times when Judge May asked you about that your answer was: Yes, you were involved in bribery countless times. Did that ever come up when Mr. Kouchner appointed you to your position as judge?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: This is what the entire Kosova knew. The lawyers, the Albanian lawyers knew that they had to bribe the Serbian bodies. It's something that the Milosevic regime imposed on us. This was the face of that regime. I will tell you -- because you are insisting on this, I will tell you about one case very frankly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: What would you think.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about that -- [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Please, if you ask the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Did you tell Mr. Kouchner -- please answer my question, sir --

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: I will tell you. I have to explain myself on this issue. And I wouldn't go ahead without explaining this. How would you interpret justice if a judge of the district court in Mitrovica who is a Serb came every day to the Albanian lawyers' offices and he came with his card for filling his car with -- his tank with petrol and he asked the Albanian lawyers to fill his car with petrol?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: My -- my one last question, sir: Did Mr. Kouchner know that you had been involved in countless bribery cases, yes or no? Did he know that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: I wouldn't call them countless cases, but there were cases. Myself and my colleagues were forced to do that because of the circumstances. It was impossible to achieve justice for Albanians without paying, and this is something that the OSCE knew, the department for the protection of human rights and freedoms. Before the war -- can I just explain one thing?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: On the 1st of October --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I would prefer that you wouldn't because we're about five minutes past our break time and if I can sum it up. The answer I think is no whether or not you told Mr. Kouchner -- you did not tell Mr. Kouchner about these bribery matters and when you question about whether it was countless, in the Milosevic transcript, Judge May said: "It is suggested that you were involved in bribery countless times, Mr. Halimi. Is that true or not?" And your answer is: "So it is and there was no escaping it because this is what the regime is like. It was impossible to work in any other way in this regime." That was your testimony, correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes, it was a regime that 97 per cent of their means of that regime was procured through corruption. They were cheating the population, they were cheating the Serbs, they were living on bribery. They were cheating their own people as well, but the Albanians suffered the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk, your question actually was not: Did you tell Mr. Kouchner, but your question was Mr. Kouchner knew. And I would interpret the answer the opposite way from you because the answer was: It was something that the OSCE knew about. Now, let me just clarify this with the witness. First of all, Mr. Halimi, was Kouchner a representative of the OSCE?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. He was the first special representative of the United Nations in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, my second question then is: Have you any reason to think that he would know of the practice of bribery that you've described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, he must have known.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And my third question to you is: In connection with your appointment, did you actually tell him that you had been involved in cases of bribery?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow me, I will make a small clarification here and you will get the answer. The UN interim administration in Kosova at that time had not established the first pillar for justice and police in Kosova. Therefore, they had authorised OSCE to collect information, to do interviews, and to short-list the candidates for judges. So it was the OSCE officers who were in Kosova even before the war and who had reports, many reports, on what was happening to us as lawyers as to the fact that we were forced to act that way, not for personal gains. Therefore, I personally and my colleagues informed the OSCE representatives what I encountered during my practice as a lawyer. We have told them even the most flagrant cases that never happened in other parts of the world. How come a judge come to an office of an Albanian lawyer with a jerrycan, a 20-litre jerrycan asking the lawyers to fill up his car? This cannot happen in any other part of the world.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Halimi. My apologies to the interpreters for overrunning our time, but it was important to complete that subject which -- on which the questions began before half past. We'll now break and resume at 11.00. Mr. Halimi, you'll be shown where to wait when the court has its break and we'll see you again at 11.00. Please just leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Halimi, the cross-examination will now continue and the next counsel to examine you will be Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Halimi.

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to ask you a few questions about your testimony so far this morning, and I'm going to try to ask my questions in a way that you can respond to them rather briefly I hope. At page 4 of the transcript this morning you testified about when you received a phone call and were told that you should probably leave Mitrovica. And then you went on to explain that the same woman who called you called you later and said: Have you left already because they have approached your home? And then you said this: I think she was talking about the military and paramilitary forces, but you have no way of knowing what she was talking about, do you? That's just a guess on your part.

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: I'm very certain because the events that followed the developments later on pointed that this belief that I had was correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But you didn't actually see anybody approaching your home or see anything that happened there, did you?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, that I didn't see anyone approaching my home.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In fact, what you said in your statement on page 5 was that "40 minutes after our departure, my house was surrounded and came under heavy gun-fire for a long period of time." That's what you said in your statement. Now when you use the word "surrounded," do you mean encircled, that there were forces on all sides of the house, or do you even know?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: After I returned in Kosova, that is after the war ended --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's not what I'm asking you after you returned; I'm asking you about what you mean when you say "surrounded." When you say "surrounded," do you mean completely encircled by forces; is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: I already said that at that time my house was encircled from three sides from the Serb forces. Now, whether they were military, paramilitary, or police forces, that I don't know because I didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And when you talk about your house coming under heavy gun-fire for a long period of time, again that's something that you're telling us because somebody may have told you that. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, was it -- was that part of today's evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It was part of today's evidence in the sense, Your Honour, he was talking about at page 4, paragraph 1, talking about the military and paramilitary forces that he thought were the ones that had approached his home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean, all I have is the two APCs that fired four to six shots.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's -- that's a different situation I think, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, indeed, but we've got nothing at all on this earlier one, but if you want to supplement the Prosecution case that's a matter for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, that really wasn't my intention; I hope that's not what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: At page 9 of the transcript today you were talking about when you were in Zhabar and people were coming from Mitrovica and coming -- actually, people from lower Zhabar were coming to upper Zhabar. And you said this: "They were telling us that the army, the police, and the paramilitaries had been expelling them from their homes." When you say "telling us," who is "us"?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Of course you know that I was not the only one there. There were many other citizens from upper Zhabar as well as other citizens who had come to that place for the same reason or reasons as myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well -- but the question really comes to this: Did anyone from lower Zhabar actually come to you and tell you personally that the police, the paramilitaries had been expelling them from their homes, that the army, the police, the paramilitaries had been expelling them from their homes? Did anyone from there come personally to you and tell you that?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: I was not alone there. It was a group of 10, 15, or even 20 persons. People who came from lower Zhabar, two or three, I don't remember exactly, they told us that citizens from Mitrovica, Suhadoll, and Shipol are coming to Zhabar because the Serb police forces expelled them from their houses. And this fact was proved later on, as you know from my explanation that gun-shots began to come from all sides. Three persons were killed, and in the afternoon, the people were made a column and made to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told us that and you've answered my question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you've answered it in -- I understand your position on this, Mr. Ackerman. But, Mr. Halimi, tell us again what you were told about who was expelling people from their houses.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because the three units, combined units, that is the regular military forces, the regular police forces, and the paramilitary units, different paramilitary units that were in Mitrovica area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In coordination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, just a moment ago you said in answer to my question that it was the Serb police forces who expelled people from their houses, and now you say it's these three forces in coordination so now I have to ask you another question. Did anyone describe to you any regular military forces, VJ, in such a way that you could conclude for certain that regular military forces were involved in any way? They didn't, did they?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: I will give you my answer. You should know that I lived in Mitrovica up until 18th of April, 1999. These forces did not come there when the NATO air-strikes began. They were forces --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Halimi, you -- the evidence you are giving at the moment is about what you were told by other people. Now, please concentrate on that; that's what the question relates to, what you were told, not something else that you can explain. This question is only about what you were told. Now, the question was: Did anyone describe to you any regular military forces, VJ, in such a way that you could conclude for certain that regular military forces were involved in any way? They didn't, did they? That was the question. Now, could you answer that specific question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In my previous answers, I am aware of the fact that I mentioned the police forces. But since you're asking me to give you a more accurate and specific answer who they were, I gave you exactly that answer. According to the information that we received from the people while we were there. I don't know if I'm clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, as I understand it, you were in a group of about ten people. Where were you? Where was this group of ten people that they were telling -- these people were telling you what they experienced?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: We were near the house where my family was staying, about 20 metres from this house in the high-ground part of upper Zhabar; that is where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Were you in a building or just standing on the ground?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: It was a kind of a knoll from where we could see what was happening in that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the people that were coming from lower Zhabar were coming up to that knoll and talking to you?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And they described the military forces how? How did they describe the VJ to you? What did they tell you that they had seen?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: They as well had received that information from citizens who had gathered in Zhabar e Ulet, and this information was that the Serb forces expelled them and made them leave their homes. I think I've already explained this. There's nothing I can add to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. So they -- what you're saying now is they were telling you something that someone else had told them?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And maybe that someone else had told the others that someone else had told the others that someone else had told the others. You don't know how many times removed this information was from a person who actually saw what happened, do you?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: With all due respect to your question, Mr. Counsel, if you were in my shoes there, you could have a clear picture. If you heard the screams, if you saw the smoke coming from the houses, if you saw the horror, you would be certain that something horrible was going on in that part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Halimi --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] People were just confirming what we could see with our own eyes from the knoll.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Halimi, how does that help us to determine who did it rather than what they did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, nobody but the Serb forces - and when I say "Serb forces," I mean the regular military forces, the regular police forces, and the paramilitary units that were working in coordination - nobody else. It is not the citizens themselves who could do this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Halimi, this Court can only work on the basis of evidence that is reliable, so we need to know what is the actual specific information that you can give us that would enable an identification of the troops involved to be made, whether there were police, army, or paramilitary, bearing in mind that all three units appeared to be active in various parts of Kosovo. So what Mr. Ackerman is asking you is to be specific about what you were told, and what you seem to have been told is that Serb forces were involved. And you've then made the judgement yourself about who these forces might be. Now, have I got that right or wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I was convinced then and I'm still convinced that no other force that could do such an activity could be taken into consideration. Secondly, the fire, the gun-shots, the detonations, the explosions in the town and in other parts where people were moving in the direction of Zhabar. And thirdly, the stories from the citizens who were fleeing their homes. I was not there to collect information. Simply, people were fleeing from their homes and they were telling their stories of what was happening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, if you're not prepared to answer my specific questions with specific answers, there's nothing more I can do about the matter. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us -- I think you've already said you were some distance away. Can you tell us -- you can't, can you, identify any regular VJ military that you could specifically identify that you saw in Zhabar, operating in Zhabar, during this time? Because I think you already told us that you were so far away that you couldn't really identify the uniforms. Is that a fair conclusion on my part?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: My first encounter was when I left upper Zhabar to join the main road that takes you to the Adriatic coast. I explained this encounter with the two soldiers. There were other soldiers that were dispersed along the frontal line --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: That is where I saw --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: -- the soldiers. That's where I saw the paramilitaries and the policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm coming to that, and you've answered my question and I appreciate it. These -- you talked about this, actually, on page 13 of your testimony today, about these young soldiers that you saw. You said they were frightened young VJ soldiers. And when you told them that you were all civilians just trying to save your own lives, you said they seemed to calm down a little bit. So it -- apparently what they were afraid of was KLA?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: I don't know to what extent I can answer your question why they were frightened. I think it was their age because I don't think they were older than 20 years. At least the soldier that I spoke with, he was about 18 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I -- but when you told them that you were just civilians, that you were not armed, that you were no threat to them, then that calmed them down a bit, I think was your testimony today, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, after you got to the border, what you told us today, page 17, line 10: "I handed over the registration plates, I handed over the ID card, the driver's licence. Luckily - but it wasn't on purpose since my passport was together with the documents of my children with my wife - when my wife took these documents out of her bag to throw them in the chest my passport by accident remained in her bag." So you wound up getting across the border with your passport as I understand your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Do you think -- I mean, I don't know what your question refers to, if I showed my passport at the border crossing or if that passport remained in my wife's bag. The latter is correct. I did not take the passport out to show it to the authorities at the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And before that happened, you say in your testimony in -- page 16 that -- line 20. The police told you that: "If we find passports, ID cards, or licences on any of you, you will be executed on the spot." You claim that's what you had been told; correct?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You didn't see anybody that actually was executed on the spot, did you?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And in your statement to the OTP of 24 August 2001 on page 14, what you said at that point about when you crossed the border you said this: "In order not to delay the procedure at the border, we had prepared ourselves by taking off the licence plates before and had the IDs ready. I told the border police that my driver's licence had been taken away before but I had it in my pocket. We delivered some IDs but managed to retain some. I had prepared to give them, if necessary, the documents for my Mercedes Benz and the insurance documents for that car." Now, what I conclude from that was you had your driver's licence in your pocket and kept it in your pocket as you went through the border. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: I already said earlier that the documents in my pocket, and that is the identification card and the driver's licence, I gave them to the police. I threw them in these chests that were on the border crossing, while the documents that were with my wife, of course I told her to prepare all the documents and told her to give everything if they asked for them. Those were very difficult moments, and it wasn't my primary pre-occupation at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well -- but in your statement you said that you told the police your driver's licence had been taken away before, like I don't have my driver's licence, it was taken away before, but that you actually had it in your pocket. That's what you said in your statement, and that indicates that you actually took your driver's licence through the border thing with you. Now, did you or didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: You should pay more attention to my statement of August 2001. I said that the licence to circulation and -- is a different thing and driver's licence is a different thing. So the papers of my car, that's a different thing, and my driver's licence is something else and I gave it to them. These are two different documents. It's first papers of the car and the other one is the driver's licence, and these are two different things.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I agree one of us should pay more attention, but I suggest it's you. All I've asked you about is your driver's licence. And you say in your statement that you told them it had been taken away from you before but you had it in your pocket. Now, did you then tell them you were lying and that you -- really wasn't taken away before and give it to them, people who had threatened to execute you if you tried to go through with the document? Is that what happened? And try to pay attention to my questions.

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: I said it once and I will repeat it again. This was a very difficult moment for us. It was very hard to concentrate on what I was doing and what my wife was doing. I thought that I gave all the documents. Whatever I had in my pocket, I gave it to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is there some reason that you have trouble answering my question? Is there something -- I understand that was a difficult moment for you, but I have in front of me a statement you made to the Prosecutor saying: I told them that I'd given my driver's licence before but I had it in my pocket. Now, my question is really simple: Did you then tell them you were -- you lied about that and here's my driver's licence or did you keep it in your pocket? Now, can you just answer that? Is that hard to answer?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: I apologise to you and to Your Honours. Maybe I forgot this detail. It's been a long time, seven years ago. But still I don't see any essential difference in this. I'm trying to be frank in my responses.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So I guess the answer is you can't answer that question, even though I've tried to simplify it as much as possible. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Regarding -- I gave my answer. This is identical to what I said in the investigation and to what I'm saying today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, with all due respect, you did not give your answer. You want me to ask you the question one more time or are you going to refuse to answer it again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, do you have an Albanian copy of this statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I do not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not refusing to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We have the English version, do we?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may assist the Chamber, I have a copy of the Albanian version of the statement with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd appreciate it if the witness could look at this paragraph. I don't know how to find it in the Albanian version. It's on page 14 of the English version. It begins with the words: "In order not to delay the procedure ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, could you --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
