utterances.text: I didn't think this was a very important thing to even talk about, Your Honour, but now that we've gotten here, I think we need to finish it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, are you able to let the witness see that copy of his statement. Is page 14 near the end of the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, it's the -- there's only one other page -- half page after that in English, so it's very close to the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Go towards the end of your statement, Mr. Halimi, and you should see a paragraph beginning with the words: "In order not to delay the procedure ..." And that's for crossing the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: To make it easier to find it, there is a time reference just above: "At 2200 hours we heard a loud detonation," and it's just the second paragraph down from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, let us know when you've found that paragraph. Have you found it, Mr. Halimi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, just a second. The court usher will now put that particular part on the ELMO so we can all see it and then you can read it to us. Now, just read aloud -- just a second. It will appear on your screen in front --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It will appear on your screen in front of you. [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's clear to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just read it out to me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "At the border I saw a big box."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, this is not the passage.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "I saw at the border a container full of licence plates from vehicles" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on a second --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- "that passed through."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're looking for a passage that begins with you referring to making it easier to cross the border, preparing to cross the border.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "In order not to delay the procedures at the border," so this is the one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, please read that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "In order not to be delayed by the procedures at the border, we had prepared ourselves. We had removed the licence plates and we had the IDs ready. I told the border police that my driver's licence had been taken, but it was in my pocket. We gave them some IDs but managed to retain some. I had prepared to give them" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Stop there. Now, that suggests that you managed to hold on to your driver's licence, and what Mr. Ackerman is asking you is to explain the apparent contradiction between that and the evidence you gave earlier today that you actually threw your driver's licence into a specific chest that was for collecting driver's licences. Now, could you clarify it for us, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I said that it's been a long time. I stand by my statement that this is what happened. It is a fact that I lied to the policemen, and I kept the driver's licence. Now I remember better. I apologise. I apologise to the defending lawyer, who reminded me of this, but what I said to the investigators of the Tribunal in August 2001 was correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And so your testimony then today is that you lied to a policeman who had told you that if he found any licences on you, you'd be executed on the spot; true?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes. At that time my life had no value, didn't have a value of even 2 cents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. We'll go on to something else now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there a number for the statement itself, Mr. Ackerman? Is it in your system or were you just using your own hard copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Just using my own hard copy, Your Honour, it's not -- to my knowledge, it's not in the system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz, does it have a P number?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, we didn't intend to tender the statement, so it's not been uploaded into the system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In that case can we keep your Albanian copy and give it an IC number?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC74, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, as you were travelling from Zhabar toward Albania, you talked about going through some check-points. And in your statement to the OTP on page 12 you indicated that "at these check-points no atrocities were committed by the military." That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: That's true. There were no atrocities committed, but there was looting and beating.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you were not beaten, were you?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: I was not beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You didn't see anyone being beaten, did you?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Where? Where did you see someone being beaten?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: At the entrance to Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Beaten by whom, paramilitary?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Paramilitaries they were. It was a paramilitary unit with an Opel Calibra.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, you describe that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness's microphone be turned on, please, the other one?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Looks like they're both on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you were leaving Prizren you say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's gone off again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- at the exit of Prizren --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Page 14 of your statement you say it was very dark so you switched on your lights, but then you were told by a VJ soldier to be careful with the light because NATO would be able to see you and maybe bomb you. And so you say that after that you mainly had your lights off; correct?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you believed that warning and acted on it to avoid the possibility at least of being bombed by a NATO bomb; correct?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Because three or four days earlier a great tragedy had happened in a village in Prizren where a tractor convoy, a refugee convoy was mistakenly bombed by NATO. And I feared that I could be the wrong target.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have one final question, and it also refers to your statement. On page 14 you talk about spending the night on the road by a fish restaurant, and you also saw some VJ soldiers there. And they told you that you didn't need to be afraid because there was no paramilitary around so you'd be safe, but to be careful of mines because there were mines on both sides of the road; correct?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have just a few questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Halimi. I'm Djuro Cepic, one of the lawyers defending Mr. Lazarevic. Today in the course of your testimony on page 5 you mention that you left the village of Zhabar by having two KLA soldiers without uniforms coming to get you at your house and they escorted you and your family to the mountains. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Not my immediate family. I explained, my brother's two sons, his son-in-law, and these two members. My family was with my -- at my brother's house. I told this to you earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: That's what I meant, Mr. Halimi. And then when you went to the hills you were there with other KLA members. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: No. There were no KLA members there. The intellectuals from Mitrovica, most of them were sheltering there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Thank you. So let's go to the period before the armed conflict began. You cooperated with the OSCE mission as a lawyer that was there in Kosovo at the time. You also cooperated with the Kosovo Verification Mission, which preceded the OSCE mission in Kosovo. You sent reports twice a week on incidents. For purposes of the transcript, could you please give a clear answer not just nod your head.

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In that capacity you sent reports twice a week about committed crimes, incidents in the area of Kosovska Mitrovica. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You also informed or I assume that you informed about the incident on the 8th of January, 1999, when there was a terrorist action in which eight members of the Army of Yugoslavia were kidnapped near Stari Trg. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes, of course. But I wouldn't call that terrorist. That's your own yardstick.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You are trying to say that this action or this act was not a terrorist action or a terrorist act; is that what you're trying to tell us here today?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: It was not, absolutely not a terrorist action because there were two formations: The KLA army, the one that captured the Serbian soldiers and the whole world knows how they were treated and how they were released, they were safe and they were not ill-treated and they went back to their families. I would like to clarify here that the highest level of the OSCE offices dealt with that case --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We have heard enough of your answer. I am the one who's putting the questions here. What sort of personal cooperation did you have with the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Excellent.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That was my last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. My name is Dan Ivetic, and I'm one of the attorneys representing Mr. Sreten Lukic relative to these proceedings, and I have some questions that I would like for you to answer for me. Now, first of all, you mentioned today an incident on the 17th of April when you said that the police came and told people to form a convoy or a column in three minutes. And I wanted to ask you: Did you personally see the police come and give this instruction or is this something that you heard from other persons?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: This happened on the 17th of April. It was about 1300 hours, 1400 hours, and I saw them with my own eyes. I was only 5 metres away from them, and they were shouting. They were not being polite. Please go this way or that way. They were shouting.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you personally recognise any of the policemen involved?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: I saw them, but I did not know them. It's impossible to remember who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you -- could you tell us how these individuals, how they were attired?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes, they were wearing uniforms, camouflage uniforms. The dominant colour was the typical police colour, blue, dark blue, and it was camouflage.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you note any badges or insignia anywhere on the uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us about any badges or insignia that you saw on the uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Here on the shoulders they had their ranks, yellow. On the chest or maybe -- on the right or on the left upper arm I think it was the white eagle and the words "MUP Serbia." This was their insignia, the insignia of the police forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, I'm sorry, the transcript says on the right or on the left upper arm. You, in fact, were showing the right arm; is that correct? Do you know which arm the white eagle insignia with the words "MUP Serbia" was located?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: I honestly say I can't remember now which arm it was, but it was on one of their arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in any event, if you cannot remember what arm it's on, you at least remember the insignia and it's this insignia that you have described for us. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes, I described it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, my colleague Mr. Cepic asked you some questions relating to the time period when you were providing reports to the OSCE mission, that is to say the Kosovo Verification Mission. I'd like to ask you briefly about some incidents that occurred during that time-period to see what you know about the same. First of all, did you have occasion to find out about or did you report to the KVM or KDOM missions anything about the 50 members of the Albanian families with the last name Shefqet, Semaseladin [phoen], and Kadrija, who evacuated and fled their homes and their village on or about the 2nd of January, 1999, as a result of direct attacks perpetrated by the members of the so-called KLA?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Could you help me, where did this happen? Did it happen in the Mitrovica area? Which village, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... village. Sipolje?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: In Shipol. I'm not aware of anything like that happening in Shipol village.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. What about the kidnapping of a local security officer Ajeti Sherafedin, himself an ethnic Albanian, on or about March 15, 1999, again by the members of the KLA? Did you know about that event and did you report that event to the OSCE as part of your regular reports on criminal acts that occurred within the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: As far as I know, we were four people dealing with various regions, different areas. I dealt with justice and the northern part of the city of Mitrovica. I knew Sherafedin Ajeti; he was the director of the prison in Mitrovica. Then he was involved in organising the local police. He was a drunkard. I felt sorry for him. I don't know where he ended up, what his fate was. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you this: In response to my colleague's question about some other kidnappings, you stated that those were not terrorist acts. Am I correct or do you consider or did you consider at the time kidnappings of persons to constitute criminal acts if not terrorist acts?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: The case that your colleague mentioned happened close to Bajgora where there were units of the KLA operating there, and these members of the KLA captured eight soldiers of the army. And with the intervention of the OSCE, they were released --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Halimi, you've dealt with that already. That's not what this question relates to. It relates to kidnapping. Do you consider kidnapping to constitute a criminal act?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Kidnapping, of course it is a criminal act. But in circumstances of war, you know, international conventions exist and when two armies fight with each other then the soldiers can be taken prisoner and they were prisoners of war. That's how I consider them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's plainly not kidnapping nor what the question was directed to. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it was taking prisoner -- taken prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe I was referring to the kidnapping of Ajeti Sherafedin what you've indicated you knew, but in any event I think I can move on. Let me ask you about two events that occurred on March the 13th of 1999, in particular, are you aware of a bomb that exploded at the fruit market in Kosovska Mitrovica in the early afternoon hours which injured 41 persons and killed three with the wounded and dead being of all ethnicities, including Serb, Albanian, and Roma. Did you have knowledge of this incident and did you report this incident to the OSCE as part of your daily reports?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes, but OSCE learned about it before me going there to the site where it happened. No Serb was wounded, no Roma. There was only one Serb -- sorry, Bosnian that was wounded. So everybody knows who did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And let me ask you about the bomb that exploded at around the same time in the Podujevo fruit market in which three more persons were killed and 23 were injured. Did you know about this incident that was attributed to the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: I have no right to react to questions of this kind, but I would like to inform Their Honours that you are offending me and I do have an answer to your question. The people sitting behind you know who was attacking and who were the victims. The same scenario that happened in Sarajevo repeated there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Halimi, could you please answer the question. It's not for you to decide which questions you will answer and which you won't; with your experience you ought to know that. And we are ignorant of the circumstances of these events unless you are good enough to tell us the information you have. Now, would you please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The explosion at the Mitrovica market pursuant to the investigations --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question relates to this: Do you know about a bomb that exploded around the same time in the Podujevo fruit market in which three more persons were killed and 23 were injured? Now, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just heard of it as piece of information through the media.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, why was it so difficult to answer that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how you heard this question that the counsel put. He said that it was a KLA who threw that bomb, and that irritated me. This is how the counsel asked the question, and that's why I asked for some protection from the Bench, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This question was: Did you know about this incident that was attributed to the KLA? That was the question. Now, you could help us by answering that question, and you say all you know about it is what you've read in the media. We can now move on to something else that may be more informative. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Lastly I have just one more -- one more incident of this nature during this time-period to ask you about. Did you know about and did you report the January 18th, 1999, rocket attack, hand-held rocket attack on a police vehicle from the Kosovska Mitrovica SUP in which five persons were wounded?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Please, if you could help me with the location. I don't know where this happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe it was within the city boundary of Kosovska Mitrovica. The date was the 18th of January, 1999, and there was a rocket attack on a police vehicle. Were there -- and I believe it was in the street of Save Kovacevica. Are you telling me there were more multiple attacks on police vehicles by hand-held rockets in Kosovska Mitrovica? Was it a common occurrence or was it just this one occurrence?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: There were other occurrences. I know about three that were -- that have grave consequences. One of these cases occurred under the bridge of the road that goes to Peje. That happened earlier. I could say sometime in 1996 or 1997 when a prisoner who was being transported from one prison into another was killed. The perpetrators were not identified --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... This question relates to a date in January 1999, which is the period we're concerned about. 1996, 1997 have certain relevance for us, but 1999 is really important. Now, can you tell us what you know about rocket attacks on police vehicles in Kosovska Mitrovica in January 1999 or around that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It happened in Shipol, that's correct, as a result of a guerilla action carried out by the KLA. They admitted to this act publicly through a communique. They admitted to have carried out this attack against the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, you stated that you had I think "excellent cooperation" with the KLA. I'd like to know based upon your knowledge and information of the activities of the KLA, is it a fact that this group was present in and operating within the city of Kosovska Mitrovica from at least the beginning of 1999, if not earlier, through the date of the commencement of the NATO air assault?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: There were guerilla units in Mitrovica that were operating from time to time. But there were no units that were stationed there. KLA units were stationed in Vaganice, very close to Mitrovica, then in Pirce village, and from there they were undertaking actions in Mitrovica as well in addition to that one in Shipol. The Mitrovica-Peje road runs in the middle of Shipol village.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And you've mentioned two areas that were close to Mitrovica. Are you aware of any KLA activity or KLA presence in the region surrounding the village of Zhabar, for instance?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How about the village of Shipol that you mentioned? How far away from Zhabar is that village or that area?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: To tell you the truth and by leave of the Bench, I will explain the position of Shipol. So at the exit of Mitrovica, that's where the Shipol starts and is about 3 kilometre long. It ends at the water supply. So depending from what angle you're interested in, Zhabar is about 2 or 3 kilometres from Shipol. Shipol is about 3 or 4 kilometres long. That entire area could be called Shipol.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And how about the village of Cicavica, did you know about a KLA presence in Cicavica?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Cicavica is a forested area which belongs to Vushtrri municipality. A small part that we call Unaza, a ring, belongs to Drenica. It did not belong to Mitrovica area.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But it is nearby to Mitrovica, is it not. Vucitrn or Vushtrri is adjacent to Mitrovica, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes, there's only 13 or 14 kilometres between Mitrovica and Vushtrri. And opposite Vushtrri you have the Cicavica hill. You have Sitnica river and then the Cicavica mountains.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. So we are talking about the same region. Now, I'd like to ask you about this Cicavica region. You have knowledge of the existence of the KLA there, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes, there were units.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now -- in fact, one of the KLA persons from Cicavica, Ismet Hoxha, was a client of yours. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Ismet Hoxha was never my client. I know him as a policeman who worked in Vushtrri until 1990 when all Albanian policemen were expelled from their -- from the service. I know him because I also represented policemen from Vushtrri in court for the violation of their rights.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I take it you have no further questions about the evidence in chief that this witness gave?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I do, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'm about to bring your cross -- I think time is running out on us for this witness so you should go back to them promptly if you have them. I've already explained there's a limit to how much you can explore KLA activity with witnesses for the Prosecution. We've got to make some reasonable balance between the time that they use and the time that you use.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I assume that you had moved from -- otherwise, I would have stopped this much earlier. I had assumed that you had moved from your questions about his direct, which you had started with.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I still have some questions with respect to the matters that he discussed in his direct as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, please deal with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'll go --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, you were asked about a trial that you sat on relative to Nenad Pavicevic, the person who was convicted of the killing of Agim Hajrizi. I'd like to ask you a couple of things about that trial and that judgement. Now, first of all, isn't it a fact that the findings of the Trial Chamber were that the accused in that case intentionally and from the base motivation of ethnic hatred killed the victims, that ethnic hatred was the motivation of these persons?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: I don't know if you have a copy of this judgement. There you would see that the crime was qualified as a murder.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that. And isn't it a fact that the motivation for the murder was said to be the personal ethnic hatred of the alleged perpetrator and the person that was convicted, in particular Nenad Pavicevic?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: The evidence brought us to this conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And isn't it also a fact that the only evidence that was actually considered by the Trial Chamber in reaching that determination was the testimony of the widow of Agim Hajrizi, that in fact three other witnesses who had been heard were dismissed as being uncredible?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: That's why the judgement for Lazar Gligorovski was such that he was released.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with respect to Mr. Gligorovski, he was released due to the time he had served and not to being found completely innocent of all charges brought against him in connection with this matter. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: That's correct. He was found guilty for illegal possession of weapons. These weapons were found in his house when he was arrested. I think he was in possession of an automatic rifle and some other kind of weapons. I don't remember all of them. And of some grenades.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And now both Mr. Gligorovski and Mr. Pavicevic were very close neighbours of the Hajrizi family. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And Gligorovski in particular, he was an ethnic Albanian, not a Serb, and he was not employed with the police in Kosovska Mitrovica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Gligorovski was a Macedonian. He was not an ethnic Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise if I misspoke. I meant Macedonian. And is it also correct that he was not a policeman but rather was a painter at the 30th July medical centre and that furthermore the judgement against him states that his neighbours knew him as a drunk who was liable to cause problems and who fired his automatic rifle from time to time in the community?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. He was a citizen of Mitrovica. I knew him from his childhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I want to ask you: Isn't it a fact that both Gligorovski and Pavicevic had prior to the incident wherein Mr. Hajrizi was killed, both had previously had problems with the Hajrizi family and had had confrontations with them, in particular with Agim?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: The reason was Agim's activity, what he was involved in.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And the other -- I think the last question I have to ask you about this and then I'll have probably two more questions on a last topic. The last question relating to this judgement that I want to ask you is: Isn't it correct that the court heard no -- the court in that case heard no direct or objective evidence linking the actions of these neighbours to any superior authorities within Kosovska Mitrovica, specifically the police of Kosovska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: First of all, all Mitrovica and the witnesses that we heard knew that Nenad Pavicevic, Boban, and others involved were never members of the police in the police station in Mitrovica. And we had evidence that on the critical night they were uniformed and they perpetrated the tragedy that you heard of.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now I have just two more questions, getting back to the Sipolje village or settlement I think it is. Did you have knowledge of attacks that occurred in April of 1999, specifically, attacks that occurred on the 6th of April, the 14th of April, and the 17th of April, 1999, in Sipolje wherein KLA armed combatants attacked and killed several policemen in each incident? Do you have knowledge of those?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: There was fighting in that part of Shipol, but there were these sporadic fighting, very short. There were killings committed by both sides. There were victims from both sides. However, the biggest tragedy is that on the 14th of April, 26 innocent civilians, young people, were executed at Kovac Street in the most brutal way.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, page 64, line 25 should read: "And others involved were never members of the police in the police station in Mitrovica earlier."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'm just trying to process the addendum to the transcript that has just been made by the interpreter. Okay. I think I'm happy with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you about -- first of all, you mentioned this incident on the 14th of April. You did not witness -- you did not eye-witness that, did you, the 26 young people who were killed at Kovac Street? You did not witness that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: No, I did not witness that, but as an investigative judge after the war together with the ICC -- CCIU --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All I need to know is you did not eye-witness it. I have short time and I have just one more question to ask you. With respect to the general atmosphere in Mitrovica, as -- after the OSCE left, did you have any -- did you have any knowledge of any animosity or tensions between the various communities in Kosovska Mitrovica, and I would remind you or remind you about the birthday celebration that you had and the telephone calls that you talked about receiving in your statement given to the OTP in August of 2001. Did you evidence any tensions between the various ethnic communities in Mitrovica after the OSCE withdrew and after the NATO bombs started to fall on Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: It was a very short time. I think it was my son's birthday on that day, 21st of March. And it was on this day that the OSCE was preparing to leave due to the possibility of NATO attacks on Serb forces. From this time on -- before this time, I would say that there were no conflicts between citizens, Serb and Albanian citizens; the conflicts were between the Milosevic regime and the Albanian citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And just to conclude, the -- during the -- during the party that you mentioned, you personally received some threats from a -- another citizen over the phone. Is that correct? You'll have to answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I thank you for the extra time, and I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there a date for that event?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe he gave it as the 21st of March in his --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, it was the 21st --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm relying on what the witness testified. Oh, the -- actually, I do have one more question on that if it was the 21st.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you -- did you report that incident to anyone in the police, given that you state in your statement that you knew all of the senior police officials very well in this city?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: I didn't go to police officials, but I went in person to see him the following day in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's the person who you believe called you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And -- and in fact he denied having called you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: When we reached the gate at the end of the conversation, he said to me: I'm sorry, I must have made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: -- was drunk.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. No further questions for this witness. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. There will be re-examination, will there?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I just have a couple of questions, Your Honour. I don't know when you would like to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll break just now I think and we'll resume at five minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz -- oh, sorry, no witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we're waiting for the witness, could I bring a scheduling matter to your attention?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could we deal with it when we finish the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Halimi, during your evidence you stated that you left upper Zhabar to join the convoy you were stopped by two VJ soldiers. I would like to know other than those two VJ soldiers, did you see any other VJ soldiers when you were joining the convoy?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes. As I explained earlier, after we left the three cars there and we continued on foot, on the right side of the road I saw the paramilitaries, while when we got to the asphalt road which we called Adriatic motorway, along the road, on both sides of the road there were police units, regular police units. So the police was securing the road.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'm asking specifically about VJ soldiers, military, if you saw any military other than the two that you described during your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: I said that the other soldiers were in a frontal line. They were lined up towards the upper part of Zhabar. There were lots of them. I can't tell you how many there were.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And as you travelled on the road to Albania, did you at any time encounter any VJ soldiers or military soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes, there were soldiers along the road at the village of Runik in the direction of Rakosh. On the left side of the road, I mean not on the road itself, the asphalted part, there was this telephone landline, the cables were there up to the village of Vitak. It's about 4 kilometres long. And I saw there soldiers, reservists.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: In response to a question that you were put by my learned colleague Mr. Ackerman during cross-examination, you stated that at the check-points there were no atrocities committed by the VJ, only looting and beatings. I think this is at 44 of your evidence today. Did you personally observe VJ soldiers committing acts of looting as you were travelling to Albania?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that's a misstatement of the -- of the evidence. I don't think he said that the VJ was involved in lootings and beatings, so I think that question is a misstatement. I may be wrong, but if he said it, I didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I think the evidence of the witness was there was no atrocities by the VJ there was only beatings and lootings. During cross-examination he was asked about the beatings and I'm asking whether he observed -- but there were looting and beating. It's at the bottom of page 49.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Then he said it was paramilitaries that did that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: He did in response to questions about the beatings. I'm asking whether he was able to observe any VJ soldiers committing acts of looting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I'll object that this isn't proper re-direct. It's opening up a new area that should have been -- if she wanted to ask about that she should have done it during direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: My silence shouldn't be interpreted as a lack of interest; I'm just trying to get to grips with the evidence. Just give me a moment. The answer was that there were no atrocities committed but there was looting and beating. And the witness said he wasn't beaten. And then he was asked: "You didn't see anyone being beaten, did you?" And the answer was: "Where? Where did you see someone being beaten? "At the entrance to Prizren. "Beaten by whom? "Paramilitaries." The answer was: "Paramilitaries they were. It was a paramilitary unit with an Opel Calibra." There was no evidence at the moment of any beatings by VJ.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: No, there isn't. He responded in a -- but I'm not asking about the beatings. I'm asking in relation to what he said: But there was looting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I think you better first of all find out if the witness saw any -- personally saw any acts of looting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Halimi, while you were travelling in the convoy on the road to Albania, did you personally witness any acts of looting?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Prosecutor. I explained this also in my earlier statement. The first looting happened in Brabonic village. So you leave Shipol, Lushta, and then Brabonic. There was a check-point there. The police was manning that check-point while on both sides of the road you could see the regular army. I was at the end of the column, of the convoy, and the distance between the check-point to where I was was about 1 kilometre or maybe more. I did not see them personally, who they beat up or who they looted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Halimi, please, we are only interested in looting, number one, not beating. That was very clear. And secondly, we want to know what you saw personally. Now, are you saying you didn't see any act of looting yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not there, no, I didn't see any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, did you see any act of looting anywhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the second --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, tell us about that then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The place where I saw with my own eyes is called Perroni i Keq. It's the village of Klina in Skenderaj on the road to Peje. There is a steep road there, about 700 metres. I saw that the convoy was stopped. We stopped as well. Soldiers got down off their vehicles on the left side of the road, on the Peje side of the road, and they pointed the guns into the cars and they were saying: Money, gold.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: What happened in this incident after they approached you?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: I saw that they got lots of money there and lots of valuables, and then they left.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Halimi.

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: The last four cars were not looted. We were in the end. We were not looted. I was not looted by anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, during cross-examination you were asked about Nenad Pavicevic, and I want to clarify something with you. When -- at the time when Mr. Agim Hajrizi was murdered, was Nenad Pavicevic a member of the police force in Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You also spoke about a person called Boban. Do you know -- excuse me. Do you know the last name of this person that you referred to as Boban in your -- during cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Maybe I'll remember later. I can't recall the name now. I remember him from his childhood as well, from when he was 12 years old. He has a big body like me. He's sturdy.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'll stop you there. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Kravetz. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: May I ask a question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: About what?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Based on this new -- new testimony about the looting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I am going to allow you to, but I don't consider it actually to be new testimony. You raised the issue by reference to a statement, and the witness gave an answer about looting and beating. And it seems perfectly reasonable for the Prosecution to follow that up; however, to avoid any sense of injustice I will allow you to ask something else about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Your Honour. I may regret it but I'll ask it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Witness, you just told us that soldiers got down off their vehicles on the left side of the road, pointed their guns into the cars and were saying: Money, gold. Can you describe these soldiers for us, please? What did they look like?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: They were wearing army clothes, regular army clothes, the uniforms that I described earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you see any insignia on any of the uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We could see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the insignia was what? Describe it.

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: It was the same insignia I described earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Describe it now.

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: I can draw it for you. There was this arched badge or patch and the letters on that were Vojska Jugoslavija and there was the white eagle on the arm. The symbol or the -- the symbol on the Serbian flag, that's the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What age were these people?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: They were young, up to 25 or 26 years old, not older than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Halimi, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming again to the Tribunal to give evidence here. You're now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for inviting me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, your scheduling issue or is Ms. Kravetz going to deal with it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Well, before dealing with that and calling the next witness there are two documents I would like to tender from the bar table in connection with this witness's testimony. They are P2 -- 360 which is request for assistance number 1097 and P 02335 page 1 which is a response to that request for assistance. I would like to indicate that the -- this request for assistance and the response deals with -- with four individuals. One of them was mentioned during the testimony of this witness; the other three were mentioned during the testimony of a previous witness who testified on events dealing with the municipality of Mitrovica, that was Mrs. Afrodita Hajrizi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe that's a document that I had objected to previously with respect to other witnesses. I would just repeat the same -- the same objection relative to the -- relative to whether in fact it can be confirmed that the same individuals are the ones that are listed and they're given the fairly common first and last names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it a document which was raised with us before?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: It is the same document. The document -- the response for -- of the request for assistance is the same document, but we have the individuals that -- or the part that relates to Kosovska Mitrovica is on page 1 of this document. It is a response to the ICTY request for assistance number 1097.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we see P 2335 then, please? Can you make it slightly bigger? Yeah, and just come up to the names. Now, you seek to present this in what respect? Don't move it, please, let me still see it? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I seek to tender this from the bar table in connection with the testimony of this witness and Mrs. Afrodita Hajrizi. And Mrs. Afrodita Hajrizi mentioned all four individuals that are listed in this document, in this response to a request for assistance. Mr. Halimi referred to the first individual who's mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But Mr. Ivetic says he objected to this document before. Was an attempt made to present this before, this response?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Not this response. I think Mr. Ivetic is referring to the response that was tendered in relation to Mala Krusa. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, Mr. Ivetic, what's your objection to this one?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, essentially, Your Honour, it's the same document and as far as I can tell it was obtained by the same means. There is no information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is a separate response. This is a response relating to four people. I don't think I've seen this before.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's page 1 of the same one that we objected to previously. The one we objected to previously is page 6 of the same document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Essentially, Your Honour, this information does not permit to us identify the persons being the exact same person because the last names are identical and it doesn't state what period of time the person who's identified here was in the position that he's in. So in that regards, it's -- it's a very open question as to what this provides us in terms of probative value. I don't know what -- to what extent the other names were mentioned by the other witness since I was preparing another witness and was not in the courtroom during the testimony of Ms. Hajrizi, but I think given the problems that we saw with the Mala Krusa response that was conducted in the same manner, I think the accuracy and the -- and the probative value of this information is likewise at issue without any -- without further information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we see the top of this document, please? Stop there. Thank you. And now can we see P260, is it, the request?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 2360, thank you. No date's given for these -- for the period that you seek information about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: No, there isn't, Your Honour. We just indicated the names of the persons that we were seeking information about. This is a standard request for assistance sent by the Office of the Prosecution, and the other replies that were sent, one of them, the one from Mala Krusa, which has already been admitted into evidence, was a response to an identical request for assistance. These were all sent out at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we consider that these documents should be admitted. The question of weight is quite another matter in view of the limited amount of information that they contain, but it's information which on the face of it is reliable and is information which may have probative value when taken along with other details from the evidence of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That was all I had to deal with. I believe Mr. Hannis wants to address the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, Mr. Hannis, I know informally we've been inquiring about changing tomorrow's arrangement so that we sit in the morning. I also know that your own arrangements may be changing so far as witnesses are concerned. So could you explain that to us, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the next witness scheduled was Mr. Dashi. The following witness is Veton Surroi who is a Kosovo Albanian politician. He's also a member of a delegation involved in international negotiations. We have a scheduling problem with him. He is here. We anticipated putting him on tomorrow, but Wednesday he has to be out of the country for some previously scheduled event. I would propose to call him out of order and put him on first thing tomorrow whatever time we start and try and finish him. I intend to reduce my time on direct examination to perhaps 15 minutes or so and let the Defence have him for cross and remaining time in the session. In the event we aren't able to finish him tomorrow, Your Honour, I discussed with him a day he might be able to return to complete cross-examination and that would be the 25th of October is his next most readily-available date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Now, if the Chamber were to sit tomorrow morning instead of tomorrow afternoon, in view of this scheduling change, would that cause difficulty for the Defence in preparation for cross-examination of Mr. Surroi?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Definitely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you would not wish us to do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, we were expecting that we are sitting in the afternoon. Mr. Hannis informed us that he intends to change the order of the witnesses and we said: Yes, but anticipating that it's the afternoon session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Well, we will sit tomorrow afternoon in the circumstances --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We have no option, I think. So the next witness now, Mr. Scully, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness is Muharrem Dashi. Given the time of the day, I probably won't make it much through his name. You want to proceed with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Dashi is a live witness. His evidence is relevant to Kacanik, specifically paragraphs 72(k), with the associated Schedule K, 73, 75(k), and 77.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Dashi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you please make the solemn declaration to tell the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Now, Mr. Dashi, you will be asked questions by a number of counsel representing the different parties involved in this case, and the first counsel to ask questions of you will be for the Prosecution, and that is Mr. Scully. Mr. Scully.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Mr. Dashi, could you state your name and spell your last name for the record.

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: My name is Muharrem Dashi.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: And where were you born, Mr. Dashi?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: In Stagov, Stagov village, Kacanik municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: And how long did you live in the village?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: All my life. I still live there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Were you educated in Stagovo village?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: I completed primary school in Stagov, secondary school in Kacanik, and faculty in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: And up until 1999, what was your occupation?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: I was partly a teacher. I also worked in a private enterprise when I could no longer do my job as a teacher.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: And in 1999, what was your family status?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: I was married. Now I have four children.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Directing your attention to May of 1999, at the beginning of that month, how many people were living in Stagovo village?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: Stagov village, according to statistics that was carried out by me and my colleagues, it had 182 households, about 1.600 inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: And in May of 1999, in addition to the people who regularly lived there, were there more people temporarily in the village?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: Yes. In May of 1999, Stagov was loaded with people. Approximately, it had about 3.000 inhabitants because of the citizens who came from other parts. There is a train station there and people were coming to Stagov due to the difficult situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: If you know, where did those people generally come from?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: These people were coming from the surrounding villages, Kovacevc Nik, Dubrava, and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: And you said they came to Stagov due to the difficult situation. What situation are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: People were being persecuted everywhere. They could not move because the main road was blocked. It was difficult for the people to get food and also there was this repression that was exercised on them all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: In the early part of 1999, was there a KLA presence in Stagov village?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: In 1999 there was no KLA presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: As the year went on, by May 1999, was there a KLA unit in Stagov village?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: Due to the pressure and considering the fact that a civilian and a person who carries a gun has -- have the same fate, the theory was that it is better to have a gun than be massacred. So a unit was formed. They were kind of defending the population from this repression.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: If you know, when specifically was that unit formed?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: About ten days before the offensive in Stagov.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Is that in the early part of May 1999?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: Yes. Before the offensive. The offensive occurred on the 21st of May, so ten days before this offensive people got weapons. I don't know exactly how, but in different manners they got weapons and got ready to protect the population as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: How many people were in this unit that formed in May 1999?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: Even in the beginnings and in the end there were not more than 11 or 12 I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: How were these people armed?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: They had automatic rifles, including Kalashnikovs and V-500. I don't know exactly the makes, but these were the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: What is a V-500?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: It is kind of a hand-held weapon, and you shoot shells from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: How many of these hand-held weapons did this unit have?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: Three.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Did they have any automatic machine-gun-type weapons?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: They had an automatic rifle and one machine-gun and one V-500. Now I don't know how to explain it exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was that the extent of this unit's armament?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: This was all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Scully, a moment ago we got the answer that there -- that they had three of these V-500s and now we have the answer that it was one. Can we clarify that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: How many V-500 weapons did this unit have?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: One V-500 and three shells. One V-500 and three shells. I don't know how else to explain it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that does explain it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: If you know, was this unit that formed in Stagov in May 1999 in communication with other parts of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: I don't have knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Besides this unit in Stagov village, was there a KLA presence in the surrounding area?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: What was the name of the unit that was based in Stagov village?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: The Stagov unit was formed spontaneously and it didn't have a name, while the 162 Brigade of the KLA Adem Bajrami was active in Kacanik municipality but in the peripheral areas. So it was later called Agim Bajrami.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Was this 162nd Brigade ever present in Stagov village itself?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: No. It was impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Why was it impossible?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: I think we should go into details to explain this. Stagov is neighboured by the main road and the railroad. The main road was blocked by the Serb forces; therefore, there was no possibility for movement of people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Scully, I think we'll have to stop there or at the next convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: This is fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Dashi, we have to stop there I'm afraid because another case comes into this court at 2.15. We've had our allotted time for the day. You will, therefore, have to return to continue and complete your evidence. That will be on Wednesday. So you should come back to give evidence at 9.00 on Wednesday morning, back here ready to resume your evidence at 9.00. Meanwhile, because you're already a witness in the witness box, you must not discuss with anyone at all any part of your evidence, either the evidence you've already given or the evidence you may give. Until your evidence is completed now, that subject is off limits for you. You can talk about anything else you wish with anyone else you wish, but you must not discuss your evidence. So we'll see you again on Wednesday morning. You may now leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The court will now adjourn until 2.15 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 10th day of October, 2006, at 2.15 p.m.
